text: A synthesis problem set spanning chapters 1 through 3: states, Dirac notation, normalization, the Born rule, measurement, and measurement bases. Every number here was already verified earlier in the course — this is about combining the ideas.

Problem one: is 0.6 ket-zero plus 0.8 ket-one a valid state, and what are its probabilities? Check normalization: 0.6 squared plus 0.8 squared equals 1 — valid. The Born rule gives P of 0 equal to 0.36 and P of 1 equal to 0.64, summing to 1 as required.

Problem two: for ket-plus, find the probabilities in both the computational basis and the X-basis. In the computational basis, P of 0 and P of 1 are each 0.5. In the X-basis, since the state literally is ket-plus, P of plus is 1 and P of minus is 0 — definitional. The same physical state gives a perfectly even split in one basis and a perfectly certain result in another. Neither description is more true; both are correct for their own basis.

Problem three: why does Hadamard applied twice disprove 'superposition is just unknown classical randomness'? If ket-plus were secretly 0 or secretly 1, applying any fixed operation would still leave genuine uncertainty — a classical mixture applied to an operation stays a mixture. But H applied to ket-plus returns ket-zero with certainty, every time, verified directly. That deterministic reconstruction only works because the two amplitudes interfere — reinforcing into one component, cancelling in the other — something a classical distribution has no mechanism to do.

Problem four: a state with P of 0 equal to one-third and P of 1 equal to two-thirds is measured and the outcome is 1. What are the probabilities immediately afterward? By the collapse postulate, the state becomes exactly ket-one the instant that outcome occurs — so afterward, P of 0 is 0 and P of 1 is 1, with certainty. The pre-measurement odds described the likelihood of getting each outcome; once it actually happens, the state updates to match it exactly, discarding the prior superposition completely.
